---
# Generated by mix plugins.sync from the Antistatic plugin; edit the plugin instead.
description: "Play a wargame on Antistatic (a forecasting sandbox: a private simulated world with its own clock, not a code environment), such as \"Wargame your life\": the user lives forward one turn at a time while Antistatic's server draws what happens."
---

Follow these instructions for: $ARGUMENTS

---

A wargame is a private run with its own clock that starts today, or on `starts_on` when the user gives a date (past or future). Each turn the user says what they do; the run's planner plans the period with its own sealed notes (your own planner subagent by default, or Antistatic's model with `planner: "server"`), Antistatic draws one outcome in code, moves the clock and returns only what the user would have seen by then. Nothing after the clock reaches you or the user.

Setup:

1. `antistatic_list_sandboxes` shows the templates and the user's runs; resume a run if they have one in play (one played in the site's chat is planned on the server: offer `planner: "client"`).
2. Start a run (not available on every plan) with `antistatic_start_sandbox`:
   - A ready-made scenario: `template` (such as `wargame-your-life`). The result carries `run_id` and a `setup` object: the premise, a bio prompt with its choices. Ask the user, with whatever your host offers for questions (a question tool, a form, or plain chat), one short round: who they play (take their own words, or draft a bio from what you know about them and show it in full; save a draft only once they approve it; or skip), and whether to keep the premise or change it.
   - Their own scenario: `title` and `premise` (their words: one line or a long brief), with `bio` if they give one. The world rules, the pacing and the curveballs are the shared defaults. Such a run is set up at once.
   - Private (end-to-end encrypted, when the user asks): follow the `private-sandbox` skill; every call for that run goes through its CLI.
   - Planner (either way): `client` by default (turn step 4): no Antistatic model calls. Pass `planner: "server"` only when the user asks or your host can't run subagents; it spends their monthly AI budget (`antistatic_list_sandboxes` shows what's left).
   - End date (either way): ask "Do you want the game to end on a set date? You can carry on after it." A date goes in `ends_on` (YYYY-MM-DD, after the clock); no date leaves it open-ended. New questions run to it.
3. Save the answers with `antistatic_update_sandbox_setup` (`bio`, `premise`). If the host already showed a setup form (a form your client asked for, or ChatGPT's setup card) and the user saved it, don't ask again. There's no pace to choose: each turn's length is chosen when it is taken. Mention once that the premise, bio, corrections and entries go to the run's planner each turn. The premise and bio can change during the run (`antistatic_update_sandbox_setup` again): each edit is logged with the run's date and turn, so the planner knows what was true when.
4. The run's questions. Before turn 1, the first `antistatic_take_turn` answers `status: "questions_needed"` (once) while the run tracks fewer than its `opening`: nothing has happened. Server-planned: make the opening set (the questions the first turns turn on; turns add more up to `aim`) yourself now as its `next` says, without waiting to be asked, researched as for any market (below); then list them for the user. Client-planned: hand its `job_id` to the planner subagent (turn step 4); it makes the set. Then retry the same `turn_id`. The user can ask for more or fewer. A question's anchors can't be changed later, and its bars resolve only from turns after it was made.
5. Goals. Runs are mortal by default: the world is drawn from the house line, and the user is scored with Antistatic's regular market points on the questions they mark as goals. Ask what they value most in the run, then propose goals among its questions, each with a liquidity (the market's budget, 100 to 1,000 points): more for what matters most. Rules of thumb: 100 for a side interest, 300 (the site's default) for something they care about, 600 to 1,000 for the one or two things that matter most; a few goals, not every question. Set each with `antistatic_set_sandbox_goal` (`run_id`, `market_code`, `liquidity`) once they agree. A goal is priced when set (each bar's house p, and their position), and its liquidity is fixed once a turn has passed. They score by forecasting on goals against the house line, as on any market (`antistatic_show_market` with `code` (the market_code) and `run_id`, then quote and submit with `run_id`): the budget is spread over the bars and decays with the run's clock, and points come as bars resolve. Since the world follows the house line, their edge is what they do: decrees and feeds can't settle or move a goal.

A server-planned run is simulated by opus unless the user picks another model before its first turn (`model`: opus, sonnet or haiku; sonnet and haiku cost less per turn; `antistatic_update_sandbox_setup` with `run_id` and `model`). After that the model is fixed: a fork can take another.

A fork (`antistatic_fork_sandbox`) copies the setup, bio included: show the user the carried-over bio and ask whether it still holds. It also copies the run's questions as they stood after that turn (with their forecasts, resolutions and goals) under the fork's own codes; from then on each run's questions are its own.

Once the setup is complete, `antistatic_get_sandbox` shows the opening briefing (T+0): pass it on as written; if `briefing` is null (a client-planned run), present the premise as the opening. Then start turn 1.

Each turn:

1. Ask what the user does this period, in their words, and how long the turn should be: `until` takes any date (a few days, a week, months). If they just say "advance" (or give no length), send `until: "auto"`: the planner chooses the end date, keeping to the run's cadence (its recent turn lengths) or else varying it with what is happening (about three days to three months), and the script's header states the date and a one-line reason (the result's `until`). Pass that line on; don't second-guess it. Never decide their actions for them, and don't suggest moves or plans unless they ask.
2. Sort what they say into typed `entries`, keeping their wording:
   - `action`: something they attempt; it is forecast and can fail, partly succeed or slip.
   - `decree`: something they state simply happens ("I have moved to Leeds"); only its consequences are simulated. In a mortal run a decree can't settle or move a goal: to change a goal's odds, the user acts.
   - `feed`: a correction to the world or its history (a fact about their real situation, or a wrong observation, with `strike` and its id); it takes no time and binds every later turn.
   - `info`: a question about what they would already know ("how much is in my savings?"). Ask these with `antistatic_ask_sandbox` before composing the turn, so the answers can shape their actions; an info entry sent with `antistatic_take_turn` is answered as of the turn's start and can't shape that turn.
   If it's unclear whether something is an attempt or a given, ask. Talk about the real world (about you, the tool, their actual life outside the run) stays out of the turn: answer it in chat and send nothing.
3. Info and feed entries go first, with `antistatic_ask_sandbox` (no time passes): pass its answer on, then ask again what they do. In a client-planned run it returns `status: "info_job"` instead: hand the `job_id` to the run's planner subagent and pass on the answer it replies with.
4. Otherwise call `antistatic_take_turn` with the entries, `until` and a fresh `turn_id` (a UUID) for every new turn. If the call fails or times out, retry with the same `turn_id` and the same arguments: it returns the stored result instead of a second draw. A failed turn leaves the clock where it was.
   If the result has `status: "questions"`, the turn hasn't happened: the simulation needs the user's answers first and the clock hasn't moved. Ask the user its `questions_for_player` verbatim, then retry the same `turn_id` with the same entries plus each answer as a `feed` entry with `answers` set to the question's `id`. If they'd rather not answer, retry without answers: the turn goes ahead on the stated assumptions.
   If the result has `status: "planner_job"`, the run is planned by your own agent (planner: client; set it with `antistatic_start_sandbox` or `antistatic_update_sandbox_setup` `planner`, `client` when you can run subagents, which includes Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT desktop and OpenCode). Keep one planner subagent per run (the plugin's `sandbox-planner` agent; in Codex, the `sandbox-planner` custom agent, or `references/codex-planner.md` if it can't connect; elsewhere, one spawned with `antistatic_guide` planner as its brief): spawn it on the run's first job, then resume the same one each turn (Claude Code: SendMessage to it) with only the new `job_id`. A turn takes it several minutes, often ten or more, and it says nothing until it's done: tell the user so in one line as you hand it over. While it works, show the turn's progress: where your host shows cards, `antistatic_show_turn_status` once (it keeps itself current); otherwise run the planner in the background and call `antistatic_wait_sandbox` (`wait_seconds` 45, `since` the last `version`) until it replies, passing on each new `progress` line as one short line and nothing else from the status. Don't poll `antistatic_take_turn` meanwhile. Never plan, read the job or look at its draws yourself, and never pass the user's chat to it beyond their entries and answers. If the subagent is gone (a new session or another client), spawn a fresh one with the job_id: the job and its notes carry the run. When it replies with questions, ask the user them verbatim and resume it with the answers; when it replies done, call `antistatic_take_turn` again with the same `turn_id` and entries for the stored result. Client turns have their own, larger daily allowance. Other players can join a client-planned game: the planner gets their submitted orders with who wrote each, and addresses what only some of them would see to those players alone.
5. Show the returned `script` verbatim, as the turn: it is written from the drawn outcome and ends "What do you do?". Add nothing to it (no events, consequences, reactions, foreshadowing, coaching or scoring) and don't guess what the planner decided but didn't show. Lost it (a new session, compacted context)? `antistatic_get_sandbox` with `script: "latest"` (or a turn number) returns it verbatim with the run card; don't retake the turn. Below it, any `answers` to info entries, labelled as of the turn's start. A script may end with Questions from the simulation (`questions_for_player`): leave them verbatim; when the user answers one, send the answer as a `feed` entry with `answers` set to its `id` (in the next turn's entries, or with `antistatic_ask_sandbox`). Then, when the result has `show`, show those markets as they now stand: one `antistatic_show_markets` call with its `market_codes` and `run_id` (one card; `antistatic_show_market` with its `code` and `run_id` when there is just one).
6. No coaching or advice on their choices unless they ask for it. The goals' points (realised and unrealised, per goal and in total) are in `antistatic_get_sandbox`; give them when the user asks, as they stand.
7. When the user says something in the simulation is wrong (it couldn't happen in their situation), record it as a `feed` entry (or `antistatic_correct_sandbox`) rather than arguing it in an action: a fact about their real situation, which every later turn keeps to, or `strike` with the observation's id to take a wrong observation out of the history. When the user's real news decides an item of a run question (a rejection, a role that won't exist), give the feed `settle` with the question's code, the item's key and outcome `no` (or `yes`): the item's bars resolve and it stops being rolled. An item settled wrongly (the planner decided the user's own choice, or misread a rejection) reopens with `antistatic_correct_sandbox` `reopen` (its code), `item` and `reason`. A goal of a mortal run can't be settled that way (it is refused): it resolves only from the world's rolls. To rename an item ("Mechanize/GDM offer" to "Mechanize offer"), call `antistatic_edit_market` with `run_id` and the item's key and new label only.

Markets in a sandbox:

- To track something inside the sandbox (a goal date, a number), make a question with `antistatic_create_market` and `run_id` (preview it first with `antistatic_preview_market` and the same `run_id`). It is simulation-only: private to the run, it resolves only from events the turns reach, and nobody resolves it by hand. The user forecasts on it on the site, or with `antistatic_show_market` (its `code` and `run_id`) to read it.
- A quantity tracked over time (subscribers, savings, revenue) is one `how_much` market with regular periods over the whole horizon, shown as a projection with fan bands: `periods: {"cadence": "month", "from": ..., "to": ...}` (month for turns of up to about a month; quarter for longer turns or a horizon past a year; up to 12 periods; the source's own cadence when it publishes less often, checked on its data page (e.g. FRED) rather than assumed yearly), not a few hand-picked months. Its `unit` is a word that labels the axis (`"subscribers"`); X is only for a symbol on the number (`"$Xk"`, `"X%"`), so never `"X subscribers"`. A value that carries over from one period to the next (the highest so far, a total to date) takes `"running": true` with measure `highest`, `lowest` or `total_over_period`, so a later period can't fall below an earlier one; a value measured afresh each period (the highest temperature each month) doesn't.
- Its starting probabilities meet the same standard as any market (`antistatic_guide` making_markets, `antistatic_market_recipe`); probabilities from judgement alone aren't acceptable for run questions, personal ones included:
  1. At least: reference classes, broad, then narrower, then close analogues, found by search rather than recalled, with sources and k/n in `basis`.
  2. If you can run code (as in a coding or work mode): make it a small analysis. Tabulate the cases, non-events included, or the series; blend the classes with partial pooling and explicit weights (a simple hierarchical model is enough); check the curve stays in order with sensible implied hazards; widen the model rather than clip bars to 0 or 100%. Put the case table, weights and a summary of the method and code in `basis`.
  3. With no precedents: Laplace's rule, (k+1)/(n+2), with the judgement stated in `basis.judgement`.
- Each turn the server rolls every run question from its house line: whether each tracked event happens in the turn (and on what date), and each number whose period ends. The script reports the results; nothing resolves otherwise. If the user wants to play in the world as they forecast it, that is god mode: `mode: "god"` (with `antistatic_start_sandbox` or `antistatic_update_sandbox_setup`): rolls then use the user's own forecast on each bar or period they have forecast (`sample_from: "user"`, god mode's default), and the house line on the rest, and nothing is scored. The mode can change at any time: turning god freezes the score (`score.frozen`); turning mortal prices the goals again, and new points add to the frozen score. A mortal run never draws from the user's forecasts. The planner's adjustments for the user's actions apply on top either way. `antistatic_get_sandbox` with `include_audit` shows each roll's source.
- The run's planner adds questions and items as the story makes new uncertainties salient, checked as yours are, and widens a how-much question whose values near its top or bottom bar or extends one nearing its end; you don't need to ask it to.
- When a new party or event joins a when-question with items (a new job offer in a question tracking offers), add it with `antistatic_edit_market`, the question's `code`, `run_id` and `items: [{key, label, anchors, basis}]`, researched to the same standard. It is rolled from the next turn.
- Other runs: `antistatic_import_sandbox_questions` with `run_id` lists the questions in the user's other wargames; with `from_run_id` and `codes` it copies them into this run as new questions with fresh forecasts. An edit (`antistatic_edit_market` with `run_id`) changes this run only. To make the same edit in other runs that have the identical question (forks of it, imports), pass `also_runs` with their ids, and only when the user has asked for those runs by name or agreed to it; never by default. The result says which runs were edited and which had no identical question.
- Public Antistatic markets are the background world the planner draws from; they never resolve from the sandbox.
- To take a sandbox question into the real world (`/antistatic:promote [market]`, or "make this a real market"), call `antistatic_promote_market` with `run_id` and its `market_code`. It returns the question's spec without the sandbox's anchors and basis, previewed as of today. Opening probabilities come from evidence available today, never from what happened in the sandbox: research base rates as for any new market (`antistatic_guide` making_markets), put `anchors` and `basis` in `spec`, and call again with `create: true`. The result is a normal private market of the user's; `antistatic_request_public_listing` asks for it to be listed.

Wrap-up: when a turn takes the clock to the planned end, a server-planned run's result includes its wrap-up (show it after the script); a client-planned one says it's due: offer it. The user can also ask for one at any time: `antistatic_wrap_up_sandbox` (for a client-planned run it returns a job_id: hand it to the planner subagent as for a turn). Show the wrap-up as returned. Past the planned end the game carries on as before; mention it only if the user asks.

Several actors (an AI-takeoff game with labs and governments), even when the user plays them all: pass `characters` (`name`, `tagline`, private `bio`, `controller`: `me` by default, or `invitee`, `open`, `ai`) to `antistatic_start_sandbox` (or `antistatic_update_sandbox_setup` on an existing run), one per actor; the user hosts. Between turns, `antistatic_update_sandbox_setup` characters with a `key` and `controller` takes a character over, cedes it to AI, opens it or keeps it for an invitee; `antistatic_get_sandbox` shows who plays each. You are the orchestrator: you talk to the user, take the turns and show the shared story. When the user plays two or more characters and your host can run subagents, give each its own subagent, started once (after its readiness check) and resumed each turn, that plays only that character with its `character` key (`antistatic_get_sandbox`, `antistatic_ask_sandbox`, `antistatic_submit_orders`, `antistatic_wait_sandbox`) and replies only `submitted`. Characters never see each other's private results or orders; you pass none of their private material to the user or to another character, and the user steers a character through you; leave a turn result's `private_by_character` and the turn audit unread unless the user asks to umpire. Take the turn once every character has submitted. The planner stays its own subagent. With one character, or without subagents, act for them yourself, giving each `antistatic_take_turn` entry its `character` key.

Other tools: `antistatic_get_sandbox` for the clock, setup and history so far; `antistatic_fork_sandbox` to branch from an earlier turn and try something else; `antistatic_rename_sandbox` names a run; `antistatic_archive_sandbox` hides one from the user's lists; `antistatic_delete_sandbox` (with the user's go-ahead) deletes it for the user (kept for recovery on request).
